1.pericope_label: Then said the Lord unto me, Go yet, love a woman beloved of her friend, yet an adulteress, according to the love of the Lord toward the children of Israel, who look to other gods, and love flagons of wine.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch set out the chapter as symbolical action followed by explanation and hold the purely symbolical character of the command evident from the command itself; Ellicott identifies the woman as the prophet's own wife, now another man's concubine slave, renders the disputed phrase loved by another against the Greek reading, and takes the grape-cakes as the sacrificial cakes of idolatrous worship and a mark of its licentious accompaniments.

Calvin insists the marriage was a vision rather than an event, makes everything turn on the verb love rather than take to wife -- God loved the people in their widowhood before restoring them -- places the prediction between the earlier denunciation and the promise of pardon, and reads the flagons as drunkenness whose craving for novelty is the standing temper of the superstitious.

Clarke keeps this command distinct from the earlier one, reading the woman as a divorced wife now repentant but not yet reconciled, the exact case of the people under the Babylonian captivity; he resolves the disputed phrase by pointing and allows the flagons to be either libation vessels or cakes of dried grapes. Wesley glosses briefly: her husband, and the feasts of the idols where they drink to excess.

Henry hears in the repeated command a rule of method, that conviction requires precept upon precept, rejects the reading that refers the chapter to the two tribes, and stands astonished that so much love should be thrown away on so unworthy a people, adding the moral that idolatry and sensuality keep company.

debates.question: How should beloved of her friend be rendered?

positions.position: Loving another, since the same consonants give friend or evil according to the pointing; the first is preferable.
Loved by another; the Greek reading a lover of evil rests on a different text.
The word means husband, as in another prophet's figure of a woman departing from her partner, and the kindness it implies aggravates her fault.
Her husband.

debates.question: What are the flagons of wine?

positions.position: Cakes -- raisin-cakes, or the grape-cakes used in idol worship and descriptive of its licentious accompaniments.
Either: vessels used for libations and drunk at idol feasts, or cakes of dried grapes, sweet cakes, consecrated wafers.
Literal drink at the idol feasts, taken to excess.
A figure for drunkenness: grapes rather than wine because gorged drinkers grow nauseated and seek new arts to recover the taste, as the superstitious chase novelty.

debates.question: Which people does the woman stand for?

positions.position: The ten tribes, since those addressed are called the children of Israel; the reading that refers it to the two tribes is rejected.
The people under the Babylonian captivity, separated from their idols yet still separated from their God.

outliers.claim: Holds that those are too gross in their notions who think the prophet actually married a harlot: the whole was a vision, a picture set before the people's eyes in which they might see their own conduct.
Draws from the repeated command a rule of persuasion, that for the conviction of sinners precept must be upon precept and line upon line, and that if one sign will not persuade another must be tried.

themes: Then said the Lord unto me, Go yet, love a woman beloved of her friend, yet an adulteress, according to the love of the Lord toward the children of Israel, who look to other gods, and love flagons of wine.

2.pericope_label: So I bought her to me for fifteen pieces of silver, and for an homer of barley, and an half homer of barley: And I said unto her, Thou shalt abide for me many days; thou shalt not play the harlot, and thou shalt not be for another man: so will I also be for thee. For the children of Israel shall abide many days without a king, and without a prince, and without a sacrifice, and without an image, and without an ephod, and without teraphim:

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both add the barley to the silver and reach thirty shekels, a full slave's price, which Ellicott reads as a measure of the woman's degradation; Keil and Delitzsch describe the ensuing state as detention rather than marriage, imposed out of affection to reform her, and group the six deprivations into pairs of civil and religious goods, while Ellicott finds the terms of the true and the idolatrous cult deliberately intermingled and reads image as upright stones.

Gill converts the price into English money and makes it half a servant's, prefers hired to bought on Arabic evidence, and stretches the many days from the Assyrian captivity through the present dispersion. Calvin refuses to read the smallness as generosity, turns the restraint into a rule for husbands against pardoning too easily, dismisses an allegorical arithmetic of the numbers as puerile trifles, reads the closing clause as the husband's counter-pledge, and holds the many days to be simply the seventy years another prophet afterwards fixed.

Clarke reckons the price in sterling, treats the arrangement as a contract with maintenance supplied to remove temptation, collects the variant readings of image against altar and oblation and of teraphim against seraphim, and calls the prophecy literally fulfilled from the destruction of the temple to his own day. Wesley keeps to the exile, where strangers rule and the conquerors allow no new images, and reads the barley as the meanest provision.

Henry gives the application rather than the detail: the people must long sit like a widow, stripped of joys and honours, and be received again at last, and are to fear not the majesty only but the goodness.

debates.question: What was the total price paid for the woman?

positions.position: Fifteen shekels of silver, half a servant's price, the barley being separate and a mark of scanty keep.
Thirty shekels in all, the fifteen ephahs of barley being worth a shekel each, exactly the compensation the law set for a slave gored by an ox.
About two pounds five in sterling, with the grain at twelve or thirteen bushels.

debates.question: What does so will I also be for thee mean?

positions.position: Better rendered to thee: the husband too will have no intercourse with her during the seclusion; two rabbis are cited for it.
The prophet is probably not included in the prohibition, his own conduct being indicated only in the last clause.
A counter-pledge: he subscribes himself her husband and binds himself in turn, so the widowhood is a mutual compact and not an abandonment.

debates.question: How long are the many days without king or sacrifice?

positions.position: Simply the seventy years another prophet afterwards fixed; the prophet does not go beyond that number.
Seven hundred years from the Assyrian captivity to Christ, and nineteen hundred more since.
Nearly eighteen hundred years since the Romans destroyed the temple, and running until they acknowledge the one they crucified.
The exile itself, where strangers rule and nothing civil or religious is their own.

outliers.claim: Turns the scanty maintenance into a rule for husbands: one who pardons at once with a smiling countenance and lays aside his authority ruins his wife by levity, while one who forgives but holds her strictly to duty shows no common prudence.
Prefers hired to bought, since the Arabic word for hire is the same as the Hebrew verb here, and notes that the Latin version rendered it I dug her from the root sense of digging.

themes: So I bought her to me for fifteen pieces of silver, and for an homer of barley, and an half homer of barley:
And I said unto her, Thou shalt abide for me many days; thou shalt not play the harlot, and thou shalt not be for another man: so will I also be for thee.
For the children of Israel shall abide many days without a king, and without a prince, and without a sacrifice, and without an image, and without an ephod, and without teraphim:

5.pericope_label: Afterward shall the children of Israel return, and seek the Lord their God, and David their king; and shall fear the Lord and his goodness in the latter days.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch argue that seeking the Lord and seeking David are one act, since the falling away from David's house was the effect of an inward apostasy openly declared in the calves, and the kingdom was promised to David's seed for ever. Ellicott takes David as the predicted representative of the dynasty, the name being used of a later house in the same way, and reads the latter days indefinitely, of a distant future fulfilled only in the Messianic reign.

Calvin reads the verse as the fruit of the chastisement -- immediate relief would have produced no repentance -- notes that the prophet says Jehovah their God rather than God, setting the true name against the Baals, declines a refined argument for the deity of the king as insufficient to settle the dispute, takes the fear in a good sense as reverence produced by a taste of goodness rather than by majesty, and dates the latter days from the grant of liberty to return. Gill makes the return a return of the heart, covering both the ten tribes and the two.

Clarke establishes the messianic reading by elimination, disposing of the family of David and of Zerubbabel before concluding from the prophecies, the facts, the rabbis and the later scriptures that the text applies solely to Jesus. Wesley states the same identification plainly and makes the latter days gospel times.

positions.position: The predicted representative of the Davidic dynasty, fulfilled only in the Messianic reign.
David himself as the only true king, since the kingdom was promised to his seed for ever and apostasy from the Lord showed itself as revolt from his house.
Jesus alone, neither the family of David nor Zerubbabel answering the terms of the prophecy.
The everlasting kingdom set forth in one person, the man himself being long dead.
Indefinitely distant, the horizon of the seer's gaze.
Gospel times.
Beginning at the grant of liberty to return home, with a continued series running from the return down to the coming of Christ.
Still future: the long darkness ends then and not before.

debates.question: What does the return consist in?

positions.position: Not the return to the land but repentance: discarding traditions, renouncing their own righteousness and believing for life and salvation.
The fruit of long correction, without which there would have been no repentance at all.

outliers.claim: Declines an argument that would have served his own side: some contend with more refinement that Christ must be Jehovah because the prophet makes him sought as God is sought, but he judges this insufficient to settle the dispute and takes the seeking more simply, as fleeing under the guardianship of a divinely ordained king.
Remarks on the propensity of some to deny the evidences of Christianity while professing to believe its doctrines.

themes: Afterward shall the children of Israel return, and seek the Lord their God, and David their king; and shall fear the Lord and his goodness in the latter days.
